title: Heinz Bodies, Bite Cells, Pyruvate Kinase Deficiency, and Haemolysis Chemistry

steps.tx: Oxidant injury denatures haemoglobin into precipitates stuck to the membrane, and splenic macrophages pluck these precipitates out, leaving cells with a bitten semicircular defect. The precipitate is a **Heinz body**, visible only with supravital stains such as crystal violet. This point is tested repeatedly because it changes everyday bedside decisions.
steps.say: Heinz bodies are denatured haemoglobin precipitates; the spleen bites them out and leaves bite cells behind.

steps.tx: Bite cells and blister cells on the routine film are therefore the visible aftermath of invisible Heinz bodies, pointing to G6PD deficiency, unstable haemoglobins, or oxidant drug exposure in the history. The aftermath cell is the **bite cell (degmacyte)**. Examiners return to it because it separates careful clinicians from guesswork.
steps.say: You rarely see Heinz bodies without a special stain, but bite cells on the film tell the same story.

left.title: Heinz body (supravital stain)
points: Crystal violet or new methylene blue

steps.tx: Pyruvate kinase deficiency starves red cells of ATP at the final glycolytic step, rigid cells are destroyed chiefly in the spleen, and chronic haemolysis with gallstones and iron loading follows from childhood. It is the commonest glycolytic enzymopathy: **pyruvate kinase deficiency**. Bedside recognition of this pattern saves time, blood, and unnecessary investigation.
steps.say: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is chronic ATP starvation of the red cell, haemolysing from childhood without oxidant triggers.

nodes.label: Pyruvate kinase step fails, ATP falls

steps.tx: All haemolysis shares a chemistry quartet: unconjugated bilirubin rises from haem breakdown, LDH leaks from destroyed cells, haptoglobin vanishes binding free haemoglobin, and reticulocytes surge in compensation. The scavenger protein consumed is **haptoglobin**. Students should anchor this fact before moving to rarer causes and exceptions.
steps.say: Unconjugated bilirubin up, LDH up, haptoglobin gone, reticulocytes up: that quartet proves haemolysis chemically.

steps.tx: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in haemolysis is acholuric, meaning bilirubin never darkens urine because the unconjugated form is albumin bound and not filtered, while stools darken with stercobilin. Jaundice without dark urine supports **unconjugated (prehepatic) hyperbilirubinaemia**. In practice this distinction decides the next test, treatment, or referral made.
steps.say: Haemolytic jaundice never darkens the urine; unconjugated bilirubin is albumin bound and cannot be filtered.

left.title: Intravascular haemolysis
points: Free haemoglobin in plasma and urine

steps.tx: Extravascular haemolysis happens inside splenic and hepatic macrophages, so splenomegaly, gallstones, and folate demand dominate, while haemoglobinuria stays absent. Most inherited defects in this lesson destroy cells this way: **extravascular haemolysis**. That is why this detail earns its place in every examination and ward round.
steps.say: Inherited defects mostly die in the spleen: splenomegaly and gallstones, but no haemoglobin in the urine.

steps.tx: Assay timing betrays the unwary in G6PD deficiency: during acute haemolysis the oldest, most deficient cells are already destroyed and reticulocytes carry higher enzyme levels, falsely normalising results. Repeat testing weeks later embodies **post-crisis enzyme reassessment**. Remembering it prevents the commonest errors made with this presentation entirely.
steps.say: A normal G6PD level during the crisis lies; the deficient cells are dead and reticulocytes inflate the result.

rows: Repeat after eight to twelve weeks

steps.tx: Trigger lists protect G6PD patients for life: primaquine, rasburicase, methylene blue, dapsone, naphthalene mothballs, and fava beans headline the oxidants to avoid, with infection itself the commonest precipitant. Giving the patient the list is **oxidant trigger counselling**. The clinical payoff comes from applying it early, before complications accumulate further.
steps.say: Hand every G6PD patient the oxidant avoidance list; infection remains the commonest trigger of all.
